summary: Works out, with a contribution from Butler Lampson, how much network capacity a single keystroke uses when a West Coast TIP user is logged in to an East Coast Host. It counts the packets for the character, its acknowledgments, and the echo coming back.

eli5.summary: It counts how many little messages fly across the country just because someone pressed one key, to show how costly that is.

questions: how many packets per keystroke on the arpanet

why was remote echo slow on arpanet
subtitle: A back-of-envelope count showing one cross-country keystroke costs four packets each way.

tldr.problem: Cross-country TIP users on the ARPANET saw bad echo response, at least in bursts.
tldr.mechanism: Butler Lampson's calculation counts the packets one keystroke causes, including RFNMs and ALLocates, and divides the capacity of three 50Kb lines by the bits used.
tldr.outcome: The network could support only 37.5 such characters per second, and remote echoing in the new TELNET protocol could have a major effect on network operation.

today: RFC 567 is a short technical note with no formal status recorded, and it was updated by RFC 568.

sections.title: One Keystroke, Many Packets
sections.content:
L. Peter Deutsch passes on a computation contributed by Butler Lampson of PARC. A TIP user on the West Coast, connected to a full-duplex Host on the East Coast, strikes a key.

The TIP sends a one-character message (1 packet). The destination IMP sends a RFNM (1 packet). The destination Host sends an ALLocate, which the author says seems to be the strategy used by TENEX Hosts (1 packet). The TIP sends a RFNM for the ALLocate (1 packet).
sections.eli5: One key press makes a small message, a receipt, a note saying the computer is ready for more, and a receipt for that note.

sections.title: The Arithmetic
sections.content:
The same sequence repeats with roles swapped for the echo character, so the exchange is 4 packets, or 4000 bits, in each direction. The cross-country capability of the ARPANET was 3 50Kb phone lines, so it can support only 3*50000/4000 = 37.5 such characters per second.

If RFNMs are transmitted between IMPs more efficiently, the capacity could at best double.
sections.eli5: Add up all the little messages and the cross-country road only fits about 37 key presses each second.

sections.title: Why It Matters
sections.content:
The author suggests this may explain why cross-country TIP users, such as the large West Coast community of BBN-TENEX users, see bad echo response in bursts: the network itself may be experiencing momentary peak loads.

If the argument is correct, the proposed remote echoing facilities of the new TELNET protocol could have a major effect on network operation.
sections.eli5: This is why typing far away can feel slow, and a better Telnet could help.
